---
title: "LLMs don’t understand the grain of your data"
date: today
categories: [data-engineering, llms, dbt]
---

When I generate an analysis notebook figure or table with an LLM I just want to
move forward with result. I don’t want spend time grading the LLM’s homework.
There’s no reward for checking the analysis of an LLM - emotionally or from my
colleagues. Sharing analysis graphs and figures are what I get paid to generate,
and the expectation with LLMs is that I generate them faster. Even before LLMs
became much better around November 2025, I knew that faster, more responsive
analysis gets rewarded over slower, more thoughtful analysis. That’s been true
of the industry as long I’ve been in it. The spend at which LLMs can generate
results, and the accompanying expectations, have just compounded this.

I’ve noticed that the pre-LLM friction of having to write analysis myself was a
form of protection. Have to type everything caused me to subconsciously think
about what I’m doing, without having to try. It was a process running in the
background. Now with LLMs that background thinking is gone. I have to do it
consciously, and I’m being nudged by the LLM not to. Even before LLMs became
good-enough, I usually felt that I should spend more time thinking ahead.

Here’s a concrete example of this from a real e-commerce dataset ([Olist][],
100K orders a Brazilian e-commerce startup). I gave an LLM the Olist dataset and
asked:

> *"Write a SQL query to show total revenue by product category and payment
> type."*
>

TODO: add screenshot image

[Olist]: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/olistbr/brazilian-ecommerce
[chat]: https://claude.ai/share/939019a5-b7d5-4516-b26e-ba987f912164

This is the kind of question an analyst would ask. Category lives in the
`order_items` table. Payment type lives in the `payments` table. Both are keyed
to `order_id`. The natural SQL joins them directly. The LLM identified a
potential fan-out issue: where the join would incorrectly create additional rows
at the wrong grain. The grain of the data, what each row represents, matters
here. The orders table has one row per order. The payments table has one row per
payment charge - an order paid with a credit card and two vouchers has three
rows. Join that to a multi-item order naively and the payment values multiply,
inflating your revenue. The LLM caught this. But its fix introduced a subtler
problem. The cognitive danger with using the LLMs is that here it identified a
grain issue, and therefore the unconscious bias is that there are no other
issues in the generated analysis. Especially when the LLM sells it in a very
positive language. If you manually checked this analysis yourself you would find
a second subtle bug that affects 2.3% of orders. Not impactful perhaps, but also
not correct, and presented to me confidently.

Unless the analysis ask is very simple, I always start with planning mode first.
Planning mode adds a little helpful friction back in: reading the plan. While
I’m reading I’m thinking and not doing. Anyone who’s ever reviewed someone
else’s, compared to your own knows that your perspective is different. Using
planning mode is a good trigger for this shift. The specifically when I do
planning mode I ask the LLM to include three sections:

- What are the exit criteria, what does success look like?
- What are the invariants and grain of the data?
- What are the potential failure modes?

All of these questions are about fighting bias, mine and the LLMs. Kahneman
might call this System 1 versus System 2. The LLM wants to think fast. I’m
trying to think slow. Including these questions almost always shows a gap in the
LLMs thinking - to the extent it makes me worried about code I generated before
including these questions in the plan. These questions often surface assumptions
that I didn’t know I or the LLM was making.

Going back to the beginning of this article - working with LLMs has become about
managing my mental effort as a limited resource. The harder I make it for myself
to check the work of the LLMs the less likely I am. And the faster the LLM
generates, the harder it gets.

## Appendix

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import pandas as pd
import sqlite3

conn = sqlite3.connect("data/olist.db")
orders = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM orders", conn)
order_items = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM order_items", conn)
payments = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM payments", conn)
products = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM products", conn)
```

## The data {#data}

```{python}
#| label: tbl-data-overview
#| tbl-cap: "Three tables, three different grains"
summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Table": ["orders", "order_items", "payments"],
    "Rows": [len(orders), len(order_items), len(payments)],
    "Unique Orders": [
        orders.order_id.nunique(),
        order_items.order_id.nunique(),
        payments.order_id.nunique()
    ],
    "Grain": [
        "One row per order",
        "One row per item in an order (1-21 items)",
        "One row per payment charge (1-29 per order)"
    ]
})
summary
```

Joining `order_items` to `payments` on `order_id` produces a many-to-many
fan-out: every item row × every payment row.

## The naive query {#query-1}

The LLM's first attempt joins the tables directly:

```sql
SELECT
    pr.product_category_name AS category,
    p.payment_type,
    COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS order_count,
    ROUND(SUM(p.payment_value), 2) AS total_revenue
FROM order_items oi
JOIN products pr ON oi.product_id = pr.product_id
JOIN payments p ON oi.order_id = p.order_id
GROUP BY pr.product_category_name, p.payment_type
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-inflation
#| fig-cap: "The naive join inflates total revenue by 27%"

wrong_total = pd.read_sql("""
    SELECT SUM(p.payment_value) as total
    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN payments p ON oi.order_id = p.order_id
""", conn).iloc[0, 0]

correct_total = pd.read_sql(
    "SELECT SUM(payment_value) as total FROM payments", conn
).iloc[0, 0]

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))
bars = ax.barh(
    ["Correct (payments table)", "LLM query (joined)"],
    [correct_total, wrong_total],
    color=["#2ecc71", "#e74c3c"]
)
ax.set_xlabel("Total Revenue (R$)")
ax.bar_label(bars, fmt="R$%,.0f", padding=5)
ax.set_xlim(0, wrong_total * 1.15)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"Inflation: {wrong_total/correct_total - 1:.0%}")
```

## The LLM's fix {#query-2}

The LLM flagged the fan-out and proposed switching to `price + freight_value`
from the items table, filtered to the primary payment method:

```sql
SELECT
    pr.product_category_name AS category,
    p.payment_type,
    COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS order_count,
    ROUND(SUM(oi.price + oi.freight_value), 2) AS total_revenue
FROM order_items oi
JOIN products pr ON oi.product_id = pr.product_id
JOIN payments p ON oi.order_id = p.order_id
WHERE p.payment_sequential = 1  -- primary payment method only
GROUP BY pr.product_category_name, p.payment_type
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;
```

This avoids the inflation but misattributes revenue for orders split across
payment types. Here's a concrete example:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-split-payment
#| tbl-cap: "An order split across credit card and voucher"

example_order = pd.read_sql("""
    SELECT order_id FROM payments
    GROUP BY order_id
    HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT payment_type) > 1
    ORDER BY order_id
    LIMIT 1
""", conn).iloc[0, 0]

example_payments = pd.read_sql("""
    SELECT payment_sequential, payment_type, payment_value
    FROM payments WHERE order_id = ?
    ORDER BY payment_sequential
""", conn, params=[example_order])

example_items = pd.read_sql("""
    SELECT order_item_id, price, freight_value
    FROM order_items WHERE order_id = ?
""", conn, params=[example_order])

print(f"Order: {example_order}\n")
print("Payments:")
print(example_payments.to_string(index=False))
print("\nItems:")
print(example_items.to_string(index=False))
```

The fix attributes all item revenue to `payment_sequential = 1`, so voucher
revenue disappears from the breakdown:

```{python}
#| label: split-payment-impact

split_orders = pd.read_sql("""
    SELECT COUNT(*) as n FROM (
        SELECT order_id FROM payments
        GROUP BY order_id
        HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT payment_type) > 1
    )
""", conn).iloc[0, 0]

total_orders = payments.order_id.nunique()

print(f"Orders with split payment types: {split_orders:,} ({split_orders/total_orders:.1%} of all orders)")
```

```{python}
#| label: voucher-misattribution

# Voucher revenue under the LLM's fix: all item revenue is attributed to
# payment_sequential = 1, so voucher only appears when it IS the primary method
llm_fix = pd.read_sql("""
    SELECT p.payment_type, SUM(oi.price + oi.freight_value) as revenue
    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN payments p ON oi.order_id = p.order_id
    WHERE p.payment_sequential = 1
    GROUP BY p.payment_type
""", conn)

# Correct revenue per payment type: each payment row already records its own
# type and value, so no allocation is needed at this level
correct_by_type = pd.read_sql("""
    SELECT payment_type, SUM(payment_value) as revenue
    FROM payments
    WHERE order_id IN (SELECT order_id FROM order_items)
    GROUP BY payment_type
""", conn)

llm_voucher = llm_fix.loc[llm_fix.payment_type == "voucher", "revenue"].iloc[0]
correct_voucher = correct_by_type.loc[correct_by_type.payment_type == "voucher", "revenue"].iloc[0]
llm_total = llm_fix.revenue.sum()
correct_total_alloc = correct_by_type.revenue.sum()

print(f"Voucher revenue (LLM fix):    R${llm_voucher:>12,.2f}  ({llm_voucher/llm_total:.1%} of total)")
print(f"Voucher revenue (correct):    R${correct_voucher:>12,.2f}  ({correct_voucher/correct_total_alloc:.1%} of total)")
print(f"Misattributed:                R${correct_voucher - llm_voucher:>12,.2f}")
```

The fix has a third, quieter problem: some orders have no
`payment_sequential = 1` row at all, so the `WHERE` clause drops them entirely:

```{python}
#| label: dropped-orders

no_seq1 = pd.read_sql("""
    SELECT COUNT(*) as n FROM (
        SELECT order_id FROM payments
        GROUP BY order_id
        HAVING SUM(payment_sequential = 1) = 0
    )
""", conn).iloc[0, 0]

print(f"Orders with no payment_sequential = 1: {no_seq1}")
```

## Proportional allocation {#correct}

The correct approach allocates each order's payment across categories
proportionally by item price:

```{python}
#| label: correct-approach
#| code-summary: "Proportional allocation query"

correct = pd.read_sql("""
    WITH order_payment_totals AS (
        SELECT order_id, payment_type, SUM(payment_value) as payment_total
        FROM payments
        GROUP BY order_id, payment_type
    ),
    order_item_totals AS (
        SELECT
            oi.order_id,
            COALESCE(pr.product_category_name, '(no category)') as category,
            SUM(oi.price) as category_total,
            SUM(SUM(oi.price)) OVER (PARTITION BY oi.order_id) as order_total
        FROM order_items oi
        JOIN products pr ON oi.product_id = pr.product_id
        GROUP BY oi.order_id, COALESCE(pr.product_category_name, '(no category)')
    )
    SELECT
        oit.category,
        opt.payment_type,
        ROUND(SUM(opt.payment_total * (oit.category_total / oit.order_total)), 2) as allocated_revenue
    FROM order_item_totals oit
    JOIN order_payment_totals opt ON oit.order_id = opt.order_id
    GROUP BY oit.category, opt.payment_type
    ORDER BY allocated_revenue DESC
""", conn)

correct.head(15)
```

## Reconciliation {#reconciliation}

A breakdown is only trustworthy if it sums back to a known total. The allocated
revenue plus the payments for orders with no item rows (which no category
breakdown can include) must equal the payments table total:

```{python}
#| label: reconciliation

allocated_total = correct.allocated_revenue.sum()

no_items = pd.read_sql("""
    SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) as orders, SUM(payment_value) as total
    FROM payments
    WHERE order_id NOT IN (SELECT order_id FROM order_items)
""", conn)

payments_total = pd.read_sql(
    "SELECT SUM(payment_value) as total FROM payments", conn
).iloc[0, 0]

assert abs(allocated_total + no_items.total[0] - payments_total) < 1.0

print(f"Allocated across categories:        R${allocated_total:>13,.2f}")
print(f"Orders with payments but no items:  R${no_items.total[0]:>13,.2f}  ({no_items.orders[0]} orders)")
print(f"Payments table total:               R${payments_total:>13,.2f}")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
conn.close()
```
